analysis.one_liner: Forces big app stores to allow outside app stores, sideloading, and rival payment systems.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2025 with 6 cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company that runs an app store with more than 100 million U.S. users and also owns the operating system — in practice, Apple and Google — to let users install apps and app stores from outside the official store, set their own defaults, and delete pre-installed apps. Developers could use their own payment systems instead of the store owner's, tell customers about cheaper prices elsewhere, and get equal access to phone features. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with civil fines of up to $1 million per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers, who could route payments through systems other than Apple's and Google's and stop paying the store owners' cut of in-app sales, and could not be punished for offering lower prices elsewhere. Consumers, who could get apps and app stores from outside Apple's and Google's stores, choose their own defaults, remove pre-installed apps, and see real price competition. Small developers in particular gain the most, since the store commissions take a larger share of their revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Developers could no longer be required to use Apple's or Google's in-app payment systems, which take a percentage of in-app sales — the main way the store owners collect revenue from other companies' apps.

Users could install apps and rival app stores from outside the official store, set third-party apps or stores as defaults, and hide or delete apps that Apple or Google (or their business partners) pre-install.

Developers would get free, timely access to the same phone interfaces and features that Apple and Google reserve for themselves and their partners, and could not be penalized for offering different pricing on other stores or for apps that connect to outside services.

Apple and Google could not use nonpublic data they collect from running the store and operating system to build competing apps, and could not charge fees or block developers from telling their own customers about better deals.
The rules would be enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation on top of existing FTC Act penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, the only companies that currently own both a 100-million-plus-user app store and the operating system it runs on. They would lose their guaranteed commission on in-app payments, their exclusive control over how apps reach iPhone and Android users, and their ability to penalize developers who sell around them. Consumers would bear any security tradeoffs from third-party app stores, since the bill says the platform companies owe no warranty service or customer support for apps installed outside their stores.

drawbacks.text: Allowing apps to be installed outside the official stores is the main vector for smartphone malware, and the bill explicitly says Apple and Google owe no warranty or customer support for damage caused by apps installed through other means — so a user hit by a malicious sideloaded app is on their own.

The bill preempts state and local app store laws, so states could not require covered companies to go beyond these federal rules — a tradeoff that replaces potentially stronger state protections with a single federal floor.

Apple argues that its App Store commissions fund security screening, privacy protections, and free services, and that forcing open the store undermines that model; the bill's carve-outs for intellectual property and security actions try to address this but cannot eliminate the tension between openness and a curated, walled-garden system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real and falls on the side of people who buy apps and the developers who make them: the bill strikes directly at the two companies' control of app distribution and payments, which developers describe as a toll on their revenue that gets passed into prices. The design is more careful than a blanket mandate — it preserves intellectual property rights, antitrust law, sanctions enforcement, and leaves the companies off the hook for supporting third-party installs. The genuine cost is security: an open installation path is inherently easier to abuse, and the bill shifts the risk to users rather than the platforms. On balance it is a pro-consumer, pro-developer bill whose main cost is borne by two of the most profitable companies in the world, with security as the honest caveat.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Kat Cammack introduced the App Store Freedom Act on May 6, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Six members cosponsored the bill — 4 House Democrats and 2 House Republicans — but the committee has taken no action of any kind since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google, which keep their app store commissions and control of app distribution while the bill sits untouched; consumers and developers have gained nothing so far.

for.name: Kat Cammack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the App Store Freedom Act and recruited its cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the May 6, 2025 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Apple
against.role: Owner of the App Store and iOS
against.what_they_did: Lobbies against app store competition legislation in Congress that would open iPhone app distribution and payments to rivals.

against.name: Google
against.role: Owner of the Play Store and Android
against.what_they_did: Lobbies against app store competition legislation in Congress that would open Android app distribution and payments to rivals.

sides.party_line_note: The six cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and no floor vote exists yet to measure a partisan split.

industries.industry: Apple and Google (mobile operating systems and app stores)
industries.note: The bill is aimed squarely at them: as the only companies controlling both a 100-million-plus-user app store and its operating system, they would lose the mandatory 15-30% cut of in-app sales, exclusive control of app distribution, and the power to punish developers who sell around them. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against cheaper apps and more consumer choice.

industries.industry: App developers (mobile games, streaming, dating, and small independent developers)
industries.note: Developers could process payments outside Apple's and Google's systems, advertise better prices to their own users, and get the same access to phone features as the platform owners. Consumers benefit alongside them when saved commissions are passed into lower prices.

industries.industry: Pre-installed default services (search, browsers, and other apps bundled by platform owners and their partners)
industries.note: Users could hide or delete apps that the platform company or its business partners pre-install, threatening the default placement that these services pay or bundle to obtain.

analysis.trajectory: With only 6 cosponsors and no committee action more than half a year after referral, the bill is likely to die quietly in the Energy and Commerce Committee unless leadership schedules it; similar app store competition bills have repeatedly stalled in Congress despite years of push.
